Guides

A pocket guide

The decisions that matter, on one page, with links to the longer explanations.

Findings

Start around six months, with iron and the main allergens. Keep up milk feeds. Move textures on. Eat together. Calmly offer refused foods again.
Leave out honey, added salt, added sugar, and whole nuts. Leave out juice, rice drinks, ham, stock cubes, and hard round foods.
Ask a clinician before peanut if eczema is severe or egg allergy is already known. Get help the same day if breathing, colour, or responsiveness changes after a food.

Do

Wait until your baby is developing the skills to eat, and start by about six months, but not before four. Offer meat, lentils, beans, egg, or fortified cereal early. Offer peanut, egg, milk, wheat, sesame, fish, and soy in safe textures, and once they’re tolerated, keep them in the weekly routine. Sit your baby upright. Add a little oil. Use herbs. Freeze unsalted leftovers.

If you’d like the reasoning behind the list, read the pages on timing, allergens, and how mealtimes work.

Do not

Do not add salt or sugar. Do not give honey before one year. Do not give whole nuts, whole grapes, popcorn, or thick nut butter. Do not give rice drinks to a child under five. Do not use cow’s milk as the main drink before one. Do not serve liver more than once a week. Do not keep a raw herb paste for a week or store garlic in oil. Do not feed from a screen or bargain with dessert.

Party cakes, chocolate bars, and crunchy granola are occasional foods for older toddlers, and many familiar versions have the wrong texture or the wrong sweetener for a baby. The recipe pages explain what was changed and why.

Ask someone

Before the first taste of peanut, if your baby has severe eczema or an egg allergy. If your baby isn’t growing well. If you’re feeding a vegan diet. If a food caused hives all over, swelling, breathing difficulty, or floppiness: that last group needs emergency care, not an appointment next week.

This site is an evidence-checked companion inspired by a Hungarian weaning book. It isn’t that book, and it isn’t personal medical advice about your child.
